entry.title: Building a Unified Deployment Pipeline: Merging Three Applications into One Coherent Site
entry.summary: This article documents the architectural decisions and implementation strategies employed in consolidating three distinct web applications. a Next.js portfolio, a React-based tools suite, and a Publii blog into a unified deployment pipeline. entry.content:
This article documents the architectural decisions and implementation strategies employed in consolidating three distinct web applications. a Next.js portfolio, a React-based tools suite, and a Publii blog into a unified deployment pipeline. The solution leverages GitHub Actions for automated builds, Git submodules for modular component management, and Cloudflare Pages for hosting, whilst maintaining separation of concerns and independent development workflows.

1. Introduction

Modern web development often necessitates the integration of multiple applications under a single domain, presenting unique challenges in build orchestration, routing, and deployment. This project addresses these challenges by implementing a streamlined continuous deployment workflow that preserves the autonomy of individual components whilst presenting them as a cohesive user experience.

1.1 Project Structure

The architecture comprises three principal components:

  • Portfolio (/): A Next.js application serving as the primary landing page and professional showcase
  • Tools (/tools): A React single-page application providing utility features
  • Blog (/blog): A Publii-generated static blog with independent content management

2. Technical Implementation

2.1 Repository Architecture

The project employs Git submodules to maintain independent repositories for each component, allowing for:

  • Isolated version control and commit history
  • Independent development cycles
  • Simplified testing and debugging
  • Clear separation of concerns
main-site/
├── portfolio/      (submodule)
├── tools/          (submodule)
└── blog/           (submodule, blog branch)

2.2 Build Pipeline

The deployment workflow, triggered manually via GitHub Actions, executes the following sequence:

  1. Checkout Phase: Retrieves all repositories with their submodules, ensuring the blog submodule switches to its dedicated blog branch
  2. Build Phase: Compiles both Node.js applications independently, with the tools application configured for a /tools base path
  3. Integration Phase: Constructs a unified directory structure by copying built assets to their respective paths
  4. Deployment Phase: Commits the compiled assets to a production branch, ready for hosting

2.3 Routing and Configuration

Three critical configuration files manage site behaviour:

robots.txt: Directs search engine crawlers to appropriate sitemaps for each section

sitemap.xml: Provides a sitemap index coordinating discovery across all three applications

_redirects: Handles legacy subdomain redirects and single-page application routing for the tools section

3. Key Design Decisions

3.1 Submodule Strategy

Rather than employing a monorepo approach, Git submodules were selected for their ability to maintain truly independent repositories. This proves particularly valuable when components require different deployment schedules or have distinct contributor teams.

3.2 Build-Then-Deploy Pattern

The workflow performs all compilation in the CI environment rather than on the hosting platform. This approach offers several advantages:

  • Predictability: Builds occur in a controlled environment with consistent dependencies
  • Flexibility: Different build tools and Node versions can be employed per component
  • Speed: The hosting platform simply serves pre-built assets without compilation overhead
  • Security: Build secrets and dependencies remain within the CI environment

3.3 Branch-Based Deployment

Deploying to a dedicated production branch, rather than directly to main, provides:

  • Clean separation between source code and compiled assets
  • Simplified hosting configuration (point to branch root)
  • Ability to inspect deployed assets independently
  • Protection of source branches from build artifacts

4. Challenges and Solutions

4.1 SPA Routing

Single-page applications like the React tools require special routing considerations. The _redirects file instructs Cloudflare Pages to serve index.html for all /tools/* paths, enabling client-side routing whilst avoiding 404 errors.

4.2 Blog Branch Management

The blog submodule maintains content on a separate blog branch to distinguish between Publii’s generated output and its configuration files. The workflow explicitly checks out this branch, ensuring the correct content is deployed.

4.3 Path Consistency

React’s build process required configuration via the PUBLIC_URL environment variable to ensure asset paths reference /tools rather than the root. This prevents broken links and ensures proper resource loading.

5. Recommendations and Best Practices

5.1 For Similar Projects

If you’re considering a similar architecture, I’d advise:

  • Start Simple: Begin with manual deployment to understand the full picture before automating
  • Test Independently: Ensure each component builds and runs correctly in isolation before integration
  • Document Paths: Maintain clear documentation of which files live where, particularly when using submodules
  • Version Lock: Pin Node versions and major dependencies to avoid unexpected build failures

5.2 Potential Improvements

Whilst the current solution proves effective, several enhancements could be considered:

  • Automated Testing: Integrate end-to-end tests before deployment to catch broken links or routing issues
  • Preview Deployments: Implement branch-based preview deployments for testing changes before production
  • Cache Optimisation: Investigate caching strategies to reduce build times for unchanged components
  • Monitoring: Add deployment notifications and uptime monitoring

5.3 When Not to Use This Approach

This architecture may not suit all scenarios. Consider alternatives if:

  • Components require frequent coordinated updates (a monorepo might be preferable)
  • Your team lacks familiarity with Git submodules (they can be tricky)
  • You need server-side rendering or dynamic routes (static hosting has limitations)
  • Build times become prohibitive (incremental builds might be necessary)

6. Conclusion

This unified deployment pipeline successfully consolidates three independent applications whilst preserving their modularity and independence. The solution demonstrates that with careful planning and appropriate tooling, complex multi-application sites can be managed through automated workflows without sacrificing simplicity or maintainability.

The key takeaway is that modern deployment needn’t be monolithic. By combining Git submodules, GitHub Actions, and intelligent routing configuration, we can achieve the best of both worlds: the organisational benefits of separate repositories with the user experience of a unified site.

The complete workflow requires minimal ongoing maintenance. simply trigger the action when updates are ready, and the pipeline handles the rest. It’s rather elegant in its simplicity, really.

Technical Stack: Next.js, React, Publii, GitHub Actions, Cloudflare Pages
Repository Structure: Git submodules with independent version control
Deployment Target: Static hosting with SPA routing support
Build Time: Approximately 3-5 minutes for full deployment

entry.title: Constructing a Minimal 12MB Operating System for Web Hosting: A Comprehensive Technical Guide
entry.summary: This article presents a methodical approach to engineering a lightweight operating system, constrained to approximately 12 megabytes, specifically designed for Internet connectivity and web server deployment. This endeavour demonstrates the viability of creating functional networked systems without the bloat associated with contemporary operating systems, whilst…
entry.content:
This article presents a methodical approach to engineering a lightweight operating system, constrained to approximately 12 megabytes, specifically designed for Internet connectivity and web server deployment. This endeavour demonstrates the viability of creating functional networked systems without the bloat associated with contemporary operating systems, whilst maintaining sufficient capability to serve web content reliably.

1. Introduction and Rationale

The Contemporary Problem

Modern operating systems, Linux distributions, Windows, macOS, typically consume several gigabytes of storage. For embedded systems, IoT devices, or legacy hardware with severely limited resources, this represents an unrealistic proposition. The question thus arises: what constitutes the absolute minimum viable system capable of connecting to the Internet and hosting a functional web server?

Our Objective

We shall construct an operating system that fulfils the following requirements:

  • Total footprint: approximately 12 megabytes
  • Core functionality: networking capabilities and HTTP server functionality
  • Deployment: bootable via QEMU or physical hardware
  • Architecture: x86-64 compatible for broad hardware support

This represents a reduction of approximately 99.9% compared to typical Linux distributions.

2. Architectural Overview

Component Breakdown

A functional operating system comprises four essential components:

Component Size Purpose
Bootloader ~0.5 MB Initial system initialisation and kernel loading
Linux Kernel 4–6 MB Core system, networking, and device management
Busybox 1–2 MB Essential command-line utilities and init system
Root Filesystem <1 MB Configuration files, web content, system directories

Total: approximately 12 MB

Design Philosophy

The approach adheres to the Unix principle of doing one thing exceedingly well. Rather than attempting to build an operating system from scratch, a Herculean undertaking, we leverage established, well-tested components and strip them to their essentials.

3. Preparation and Environment Setup

Prerequisites

Before commencing, ensure your development system possesses:

  • A Linux-based development environment (Ubuntu, Debian, or similar)
  • Approximately 2–3 gigabytes of free disk space for compilation artefacts
  • Essential build tools: gcc, make, git, wget
  • Moderate technical proficiency with command-line interfaces

Establishing the Build Environment

# Install requisite dependencies
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential wget git bc ncurses-dev \
  flex bison openssl libssl-dev libelf-dev libdw-dev \
  binutils-dev nasm mtools qemu-system-x86

# Establish project directory structure
mkdir -p ~/minimal-os/{kernel,busybox,syslinux,rootfs/{boot,www,etc,proc,sys,dev}}
cd ~/minimal-os

This foundational step ensures all necessary tools are available for subsequent compilation tasks.

4. Linux Kernel Compilation

Kernel Selection and Download

The Linux kernel, the heart of any Linux-based operating system, must be compiled with minimal configuration to reduce its footprint.

cd ~/minimal-os/kernel
wget https://www.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/v6.x/linux-6.1.158.tar.xz
tar xf linux-6.1.158.tar.xz
cd linux-6.1.158

Kernel Configuration Strategy

Rather than including drivers for every conceivable device, we shall configure the kernel exclusively for:

  • Networking capabilities (essential for Internet connectivity)
  • Virtual block devices (e.g., SATA, virtio for QEMU compatibility)
  • ext4 filesystem support
  • Serial console output (invaluable for debugging)
# Generate minimal configuration
cat > .config << 'EOF'
CONFIG_64BIT=y
CONFIG_X86=y
CONFIG_KERNEL_GZIP=y
CONFIG_SERIAL_8250=y
CONFIG_SERIAL_8250_CONSOLE=y
CONFIG_NET=y
CONFIG_INET=y
CONFIG_NETDEVICES=y
CONFIG_NET_CORE=y
CONFIG_E1000=y
CONFIG_VIRTIO_NET=y
CONFIG_EXT4_FS=y
CONFIG_SYSVIPC=n
CONFIG_SYSFS=y
CONFIG_PROC_FS=y
CONFIG_DEVTMPFS=y
CONFIG_DEVTMPFS_MOUNT=y
CONFIG_UNIX=y
CONFIG_MODULES=n
CONFIG_DEBUG_KERNEL=n
CONFIG_STRIP_ASM_SYMS=y
EOF

# Populate remaining configuration with sensible defaults
make olddefconfig

# Initiate compilation
make -j$(nproc)

# Verify kernel size
ls -lh arch/x86/boot/bzImage

Expected outcome: A kernel binary of 4–6 MB.

Compilation Considerations

The -j$(nproc) flag parallelises compilation across available CPU cores, significantly reducing compilation time. On modern hardware, anticipate 10–30 minutes of compilation time.

Advisory note: Should compilation failures occur, ensure all prerequisite libraries are installed. The libelf-dev and libdw-dev packages are frequently overlooked yet essential.

5. Busybox: The Swiss Army Knife

Understanding Busybox

Busybox consolidates numerous Unix utilities into a single, statically-linked binary. Rather than maintaining separate executables for ls, cat, cp, et cetera, Busybox provides all functionality within approximately 1–2 megabytes.

Busybox Configuration

cd ~/minimal-os/busybox
wget https://busybox.net/downloads/busybox-1.36.1.tar.bz2
tar xf busybox-1.36.1.tar.bz2
cd busybox-1.36.1

# Apply minimal configuration
cat > .config << 'EOF'
CONFIG_SH_ASH=y
CONFIG_INIT=y
CONFIG_MOUNT=y
CONFIG_UMOUNT=y
CONFIG_HOSTNAME=y
CONFIG_IFCONFIG=y
CONFIG_PING=y
CONFIG_ROUTE=y
CONFIG_DHCPC=y
CONFIG_WGET=y
CONFIG_HTTPD=y
CONFIG_HTTPD_PORT=80
CONFIG_LS=y
CONFIG_CP=y
CONFIG_MV=y
CONFIG_RM=y
CONFIG_MKDIR=y
CONFIG_CAT=y
CONFIG_ECHO=y
CONFIG_FIND=y
CONFIG_STATIC=y
EOF

# Compile with static linking
make oldconfig
make -j$(nproc) LDFLAGS="-static"

# Verify binary size
ls -lh busybox

Static linking ensures the binary operates independently, without requiring shared libraries. This is critical for embedded systems.

6. Root Filesystem Construction

Directory Structure Establishment

cd ~/minimal-os/rootfs

# Create essential directories
mkdir -p {bin,sbin,etc,proc,sys,dev,var,tmp,www,boot/syslinux}

# Copy compiled binaries
cp ~/minimal-os/kernel/linux-6.1.158/arch/x86/boot/bzImage boot/kernel
cp ~/minimal-os/busybox/busybox-1.36.1/busybox bin/

# Create symbolic link
cd bin && ln -s busybox sh && cd ..

System Initialisation Scripts

# Create init script
cat > etc/init.d/rcS << 'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
mount -t proc none /proc
mount -t sysfs none /sys
mount -t devtmpfs none /dev
hostname minimal-web-server
echo "Minimal Web OS Initialising..."
ifconfig lo 127.0.0.1
udhcpc -i eth0 &
/bin/busybox httpd -h /www
EOF

chmod +x etc/init.d/rcS

# Create inittab configuration
cat > etc/inittab << 'EOF'
::sysinit:/etc/init.d/rcS
::askfirst:/bin/sh
::ctrlaltdel:/bin/umount -a -r
EOF

# System user files
cat > etc/passwd << 'EOF'
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh
EOF

cat > etc/group << 'EOF'
root:x:0:
EOF

Web Content

# Create sample webpage
cat > www/index.html << 'EOF'
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Minimal Web Server</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: 'Segoe UI', Tahoma, Geneva, Verdana, sans-serif; 
               background: linear-gradient(135deg, #667eea 0%, #764ba2 100%); 
               padding: 20px; margin: 0; }
        .container { max-width: 600px; margin: 0 auto; 
                    background: white; padding: 30px; border-radius: 8px; 
                    box-shadow: 0 10px 25px rgba(0,0,0,0.2); }
        h1 { color: #333; margin-top: 0; }
        .status { background: #d4edda; color: #155724; 
                 padding: 15px; border-radius: 4px; }
        p { color: #666; line-height: 1.6; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <div class="container">
        <h1>✓ Minimal Operating System</h1>
        <div class="status">
            <strong>Status:</strong> Web server operational
        </div>
        <p>This server is executing upon a custom-engineered minimal Linux operating system, constrained to approximately 12 megabytes.</p>
        <p><strong>System Specifications:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Total OS size: ~12 MB</li>
            <li>Kernel: Linux 6.1.158 (minimal configuration)</li>
            <li>Utilities: Busybox 1.36.1</li>
            <li>Web Server: Busybox httpd</li>
            <li>Filesystem: ext4</li>
        </ul>
    </div>
</body>
</html>
EOF

7. Bootloader Installation

Syslinux: The Boot Manager

Syslinux provides a lightweight bootloader capable of loading and executing the Linux kernel.

cd ~/minimal-os/syslinux
wget https://mirrors.edge.kernel.org/pub/linux/utils/boot/syslinux/syslinux-6.03.tar.gz
tar xf syslinux-6.03.tar.gz
cd syslinux-6.03

# Compile Syslinux
make -j$(nproc)

# Locate the bootloader binary
find . -name "syslinux.bin" -type f

Boot Configuration

cd ~/minimal-os/rootfs/boot/syslinux

cat > syslinux.cfg << 'EOF'
PROMPT 1
TIMEOUT 50
DEFAULT linux

LABEL linux
    KERNEL /boot/kernel
    APPEND root=/dev/sda1 console=ttyS0 console=tty0 quiet
EOF

8. Creating the Bootable Disk Image

Disk Image Generation

cd ~/minimal-os

# Create 12 MB raw disk image
dd if=/dev/zero of=disk.img bs=1M count=12

# Create partition table
(echo o; echo n; echo p; echo 1; echo ; echo ; echo w) | fdisk disk.img

# Establish loop device
LOOP=$(sudo losetup -f)
sudo losetup $LOOP disk.img -o 1048576

# Format partition
sudo mkfs.ext4 -F $LOOP

# Mount and populate
mkdir -p mnt
sudo mount $LOOP mnt
sudo cp -r rootfs/* mnt/
sudo sync
sudo umount mnt

# Install bootloader
SYSLINUX_BIN=$(find syslinux/syslinux-6.03 -name "syslinux.bin" -type f | head -1)
sudo dd if=$SYSLINUX_BIN of=disk.img bs=1 count=440 conv=notrunc

# Finalisation
sudo losetup -d $LOOP

# Verification
ls -lh disk.img

9. Deployment and Testing

QEMU Emulation (Recommended)

For initial testing, QEMU provides a safe, isolated environment:

qemu-system-x86_64 -drive file=disk.img,format=raw \
  -m 256 \
  -netdev user,id=net0 \
  -device e1000,netdev=net0 \
  -nographic \
  -serial mon:stdio

Expected Behaviour

Upon boot, you should observe:

  1. Bootloader initialisation via Syslinux
  2. Kernel loading and initialisation messages
  3. Network interface configuration via DHCP
  4. Web server activation on port 80
  5. System ready for incoming HTTP requests

Testing Connectivity

# From your host system (in another terminal)
# If using QEMU user networking, access at localhost

# Get IP from QEMU output, then:
curl http://192.168.x.x
# Should return your HTML page

Physical Hardware Deployment (Advanced)

Caution: This operation will overwrite your target storage device.

# Write to USB drive (replace sdX with your device)
sudo dd if=disk.img of=/dev/sdX bs=4M conv=fsync
sudo sync

10. Optimisation and Troubleshooting

Size Reduction Strategies

Should your system exceed 12 MB, consider:

  1. Binary stripping: strip ~/minimal-os/rootfs/bin/busybox
  2. Kernel compression: Enable XZ compression in CONFIG_KERNEL_XZ
  3. Minimal configuration: Disable unused Busybox utilities
  4. Filesystem optimisation: Remove unnecessary files from /var

Common Issues and Remedies

Issue Solution
Kernel fails to compile Reinstall libelf-dev, libdw-dev
Network unreachable Verify CONFIG_NETDEVICES=y and CONFIG_E1000=y
Web server won’t start Check /www/index.html exists and permissions
Boot hangs at Syslinux Verify kernel path in syslinux.cfg is correct
Filesystem corruption Regenerate disk image from scratch

11. Conclusions and Future Considerations

Achievements

Through this exercise, we have demonstrated:

  • The viability of creating functional operating systems at minimal scale
  • The efficacy of leveraging established open-source components
  • The potential for deploying systems on severely constrained hardware

Practical Applications

Such minimalist systems prove invaluable for:

  • Embedded IoT devices
  • Legacy hardware revitalisation
  • Disaster recovery and minimal boot environments
  • Educational purposes and systems programming study
  • Network-attached storage (NAS) on minimal hardware

Further Enhancements

For production deployment, one might consider:

  • Integration with Docker for containerised applications
  • Implementation of systemd for more sophisticated service management
  • SSL/TLS support for secure web communications
  • Database integration for dynamic content generation
  • Automated deployment via cloud-init or similar technologies

12. Final Remarks

The construction of a minimal operating system represents not merely a technical exercise, but a valuable reminder that contemporary bloat is not inevitable. By understanding the constituent components of an operating system and making deliberate design choices, one can create systems that are simultaneously powerful and parsimonious in their resource consumption.

This approach, building only what is necessary, remains a cornerstone principle of excellent engineering, whether applied to operating systems, software architecture, or infrastructure design.

Appendix A: Complete Build Script

For those preferring automation:

#!/bin/bash
set -e

cd ~/minimal-os

echo "=== Compiling Linux Kernel ==="
cd kernel/linux-6.1.158
make -j$(nproc)
cp arch/x86/boot/bzImage ../../../rootfs/boot/kernel

echo "=== Compiling Busybox ==="
cd ~/minimal-os/busybox/busybox-1.36.1
make -j$(nproc) LDFLAGS="-static"
cp busybox ../../rootfs/bin/
cd ../../rootfs/bin && ln -sf busybox sh

echo "=== Building Syslinux ==="
cd ~/minimal-os/syslinux/syslinux-6.03
make -j$(nproc)

echo "=== Creating Disk Image ==="
cd ~/minimal-os
dd if=/dev/zero of=disk.img bs=1M count=12
(echo o; echo n; echo p; echo 1; echo ; echo ; echo w) | fdisk disk.img

LOOP=$(sudo losetup -f)
sudo losetup $LOOP disk.img -o 1048576
sudo mkfs.ext4 -F $LOOP
mkdir -p mnt
sudo mount $LOOP mnt
sudo cp -r rootfs/* mnt/
sudo sync
sudo umount mnt

SYSLINUX_BIN=$(find syslinux/syslinux-6.03 -name "syslinux.bin" | head -1)
sudo dd if=$SYSLINUX_BIN of=disk.img bs=1 count=440 conv=notrunc
sudo losetup -d $LOOP

echo "✓ Build complete!"
ls -lh disk.img

References

  • Linux Kernel Documentation: https://www.kernel.org/doc/
  • Busybox Project: https://busybox.net/
  • Syslinux Project: https://syslinux.org/
  • QEMU Documentation: https://www.qemu.org/documentation/

entry.title: How to Use Discord Webhook with Examples: The Ultimate Step-by-Step Guide
entry.summary: Introduction to Discord Webhooks Discord has grown beyond a simple voice chat platform into a full-fledged community hub for gamers, developers, and businesses alike. One of the most powerful tools it offers is webhooks. But what exactly are Discord webhooks, and how can you use…
entry.content:
Introduction to Discord Webhooks

Discord has grown beyond a simple voice chat platform into a full-fledged community hub for gamers, developers, and businesses alike. One of the most powerful tools it offers is webhooks.

But what exactly are Discord webhooks, and how can you use them effectively? Whether you’re a beginner looking to send automated notifications or a developer integrating external apps, this guide will walk you through everything you need to know—complete with practical examples.

What Are Discord Webhooks?

At its core, a Discord webhook is a way for external applications to send messages into a Discord channel automatically. Instead of typing a message yourself, you can configure apps or scripts to push content directly into your server.

In simpler terms, think of webhooks as automated messengers that can deliver updates, alerts, or notifications straight into your community.

Why Use Discord Webhooks?

Some of the most common reasons people use Discord webhooks include:

  • Automated Notifications – Get alerts when a new commit is pushed on GitHub or when your server goes down.

  • Integration with External Apps – Connect platforms like Trello, GitHub, or Jenkins with your Discord server.

  • Custom Announcements – Post updates from a website, blog, or bot without manual input.

Benefits of Discord Webhooks for Developers and Communities

  • Saves time with automation

  • Improves communication in communities

  • Provides real-time monitoring (e.g., error alerts, API logs)

  • Easy to set up without coding knowledge

Setting Up a Discord Webhook

Prerequisites Before Creating a Webhook

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • A Discord server where you have Manage Webhooks permission

  • A channel where notifications will be posted

  • Basic familiarity with copy-pasting links

Step-by-Step Guide to Creating a Webhook in Discord

  1. Open Server Settings in Discord.

  2. Select Integrations → Webhooks.

  3. Click New Webhook.

  4. Give your webhook a name and assign it to a channel.

  5. Copy the Webhook URL—this is what you’ll use to send data.

Managing and Customizing Your Webhook

You can:

  • Assign an avatar (custom profile picture)

  • Change its posting channel anytime

  • Rename the webhook for different use cases

How Discord Webhooks Work Internally

Anatomy of a Webhook URL

A Discord webhook URL looks like this:

https://discord.com/api/webhooks/{webhook.id}/{webhook.token}

Both the ID and Token must be kept secure, as anyone with this link can post messages to your channel.

Supported Data Formats (JSON & Embeds)

  • Plain text messages – Quick updates

  • JSON payloads – Structured data

  • Embeds – Rich content with titles, descriptions, images, and fields

Sending Messages with Discord Webhooks

Sending a Simple Text Message via cURL

curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"content":"Hello from Discord Webhook!"}' \
https://discord.com/api/webhooks/WEBHOOK_ID/WEBHOOK_TOKEN

Sending JSON Payloads with Custom Formatting

{
  "content": "New update available!",
  "username": "Update Bot",
  "avatar_url": "https://example.com/avatar.png"
}

Adding Embeds for Rich Content

{
  "embeds": [{
    "title": "Server Status",
    "description": "✅ All systems operational",
    "color": 65280
  }]
}

Practical Examples of Using Discord Webhooks

Example 1: GitHub Push Notifications

In your GitHub repository, go to Settings → Webhooks → Add Webhook.

Paste your Discord Webhook URL into the “Payload URL” field.

Set the Content type to application/json and choose which events you’d like (e.g., push, pull_request, or issues).

Now, whenever someone pushes new code, merges a pull request, or opens an issue, Discord will automatically post a structured message in your chosen channel.

This makes it easy for your whole team to stay up-to-date on changes without leaving Discord.

Example 2: Server Monitoring Alerts

Use free uptime monitoring services like UptimeRobot, BetterUptime, or even custom scripts running on your server.

Configure these tools to send alerts to your Discord Webhook if your website or application goes offline, response times spike, or critical errors occur.

You can customize alert frequency (e.g., every 5 minutes if downtime persists) and format the message to include server name, timestamp, and current status.

This ensures your team gets real-time alerts directly in Discord, making it easier to respond quickly without having to constantly check dashboards.

Example 3: Custom Bot-like Notifications

Even without coding a bot, Discord webhooks allow you to send styled messages using JSON payloads.

You can customize:

Username & Avatar → Make messages appear as if they came from a bot or a custom account.

Rich Embeds → Add colored sidebars, bold titles, clickable links, images, and even fields with structured data.

Timestamps → Automatically show when an event occurred.

Example: You could create a webhook that posts a daily summary like:

“✅ All systems running smoothly”

“⚠️ Warning: Disk usage at 85%”

This makes the webhook feel like a lightweight bot, perfect for dashboards, reminders, or project updates without needing to host or code a full bot.

Advanced Webhook Features

Discord webhooks may seem simple at first glance, but they offer powerful features when combined with external scripts and automation tools. Let’s break down some advanced capabilities.

Using Multiple Webhooks in One Channel

  • A single channel can have multiple webhooks assigned.

  • This is useful if you want different integrations—for example:

    • One webhook for GitHub updates

    • Another webhook for server monitoring

    • A third webhook for announcements

Pro Tip: Assign unique usernames and avatars to differentiate which webhook sent the message.

Automating Webhooks with Python or Node.js

Instead of manually using cURL, you can integrate webhooks into scripts or applications.

Example: Sending a Message with Python (using requests)

import requests

url = "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/WEBHOOK_ID/WEBHOOK_TOKEN"
data = {
    "content": "Hello from Python!",
    "username": "Python Bot"
}

response = requests.post(url, json=data)
print(response.status_code)

Example: Sending a Message with Node.js

const fetch = require("node-fetch");

const url = "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/WEBHOOK_ID/WEBHOOK_TOKEN";

const data = {
  content: "Hello from Node.js!",
  username: "Node Bot"
};

fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(data)
})
.then(res => console.log(res.status));

With these, you can automate alerts, reminders, and event notifications.

Rate Limits and Best Practices

Discord webhooks are subject to rate limits to prevent spam:

  • Maximum of 5 requests per second per webhook

  • Payload size should not exceed 8 MB

Best Practices:

  • Bundle multiple messages into a single embed instead of spamming

  • Don’t expose your webhook URL in public code repositories

  • Use environment variables for storing webhook tokens securely

Security Considerations for Discord Webhooks

Protecting Your Webhook URL

Anyone with your webhook URL can post messages in your channel. To secure it:

  • Never share the URL publicly

  • Store it in a safe location (e.g., .env file for projects)

  • Regenerate the webhook if you suspect it has been compromised

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Posting sensitive information (passwords, API keys) through webhooks

  • Forgetting to set the Content-Type header as application/json

  • Ignoring rate limits, which may result in failed requests

Troubleshooting Common Webhook Issues

Why Is My Webhook Not Sending?

Common reasons include:

  • Invalid webhook URL (copied incorrectly)

  • Missing Content-Type header

  • JSON payload formatting errors

Debugging JSON Payload Errors

If Discord rejects your request, double-check:

  • Brackets {} and arrays [] are properly closed

  • Field names are lowercase (e.g., "content", not "Content")

  • Payload size does not exceed 8 MB

You can validate JSON at https://jsonlint.com.

FAQs About Discord Webhooks

Can I use Discord webhooks without a bot?

Yes! Unlike bots, webhooks don’t require coding or OAuth2 setup. You simply paste the webhook URL into your script or integration tool.

What is the message limit for webhooks?

Each webhook message can have up to 2000 characters in plain text or 6000 characters if using embeds.

How many webhooks can a channel have?

A single channel can have up to 10 webhooks.

Can I edit or delete webhook messages?

Yes. Webhooks can edit or delete their own messages, but not those of other webhooks or users.

Are Discord webhooks free to use?

Absolutely! Discord provides webhooks free of charge, making them accessible to all communities and developers.

Can I schedule webhook messages?

Not directly. However, you can schedule them using cron jobs in Linux or third-party automation tools like Zapier or IFTTT.

Conclusion

Discord webhooks are one of the most powerful yet underrated features of the platform. Whether you’re a developer seeking real-time integrations or a community admin who wants automated updates, webhooks can save time, improve communication, and enhance engagement.

By following this guide, you’ve learned:

  • What Discord webhooks are and why they’re useful

  • How to create and customize them

  • How to send messages using cURL, JSON, Python, and Node.js

  • Advanced features like embeds, automation, and security best practices

  • Real-world examples for GitHub, monitoring, and notifications

So go ahead—set up your own webhook today and unlock the full potential of Discord automation. 🚀

entry.title: Recovering Deleted Files from Encrypted rclone Backups
entry.summary: Accidentally deleting a file from a production system can happen to anyone — a misplaced rm -rf, an accidental overwrite, or even a CMS update gone wrong. If you’ve been running automated rclone backups with encryption via rclone crypt, you have a powerful safety net.
entry.content:
Accidentally deleting a file from a production system can happen to anyone — a misplaced rm -rf, an accidental overwrite, or even a CMS update gone wrong. If you’ve been running automated rclone backups with encryption via rclone crypt, you have a powerful safety net.

In this guide, we’ll walk through:

  • How encrypted rclone backups work
  • How to verify your encrypted remote is working
  • How to search for and locate deleted files
  • How to restore them safely without breaking your live environment
  • Best practices for making future recoveries faster

1. Understanding Your Encrypted Backup Setup

When you use rclone crypt, you are not uploading raw files. Instead:

  1. Files are encrypted locally before leaving your machine
  2. Filenames and directory names are also scrambled (optional but recommended)
  3. The remote cloud storage provider only sees random binary data
  4. rclone decrypts transparently when you access the remote through the crypt configuration

A typical configuration involves two remotes:

  • A base remote — e.g., an S3 bucket, Google Drive, etc.
  • A crypt remote — pointing to a folder inside the base remote, where encryption is applied

Example from rclone.conf:

[my-backup]
type = s3
provider = Other
access_key_id = ********
secret_access_key = ********
endpoint = https://s3.example.com

[my-backup-crypt]
type = crypt
remote = my-backup:encrypted-storage
password = <encrypted-password>
password2 = <encrypted-salt>

With this setup, all operations happen on my-backup-crypt:, but the physical data is stored encrypted inside my-backup:. a complete indepth guide here

2. Confirming the File Exists in Backup

When a file is deleted locally, your backup may still contain it — unless it has already been overwritten by a sync operation.

Step 1 — List the folder where you expect the file to be:

rclone --config=/path/to/rclone.conf ls my-backup-crypt:backups/var-www/html/

If the file is present, it will appear in the output along with its size.

Step 2 — Search the entire backup if unsure:

rclone --config=/path/to/rclone.conf ls my-backup-crypt:backups | grep index.php

This works even with encrypted remotes because rclone will decrypt filenames before showing them (as long as you’re accessing via the crypt remote).

3. Restoring a Deleted File

Once you’ve confirmed the file exists, restoring it is straightforward.

Restore to the original location:

rclone --config=/path/to/rclone.conf copy my-backup-crypt:backups/var-www/html/index.php /var/www/html/ -P

Restore to a safe temporary folder first (recommended for production):

mkdir -p /tmp/recovery-test
rclone --config=/path/to/rclone.conf copy my-backup-crypt:backups/var-www/html/index.php /tmp/recovery-test -P

Once you confirm the file integrity, you can move it back into production.

4. Handling Versioned or Snapshot Backups

If your backup strategy uses dated snapshots (e.g., /backups/2025-08-10/var-www/...), you can recover older versions:

rclone --config=/path/to/rclone.conf copy my-backup-crypt:backups/2025-08-01/var-www/html/index.php /var/www/html/ -P

Snapshots are especially useful when a bad file sync might have overwritten the good copy in your main backup folder.

5. Troubleshooting Common Recovery Issues

File Not Found

  • Check if your backup script used sync instead of copy — sync can delete files from the remote if they are deleted locally.
  • Look inside older dated snapshot folders.

Permission Errors

  • Run with sudo if restoring to system-owned directories (e.g., /etc, /var/www).

  • Example:

    sudo rclone --config=/path/to/rclone.conf copy ...

Wrong Config

  • Ensure you’re using the correct rclone.conf that contains your crypt remote configuration.

  • Example:

    rclone --config=/root/.config/rclone/rclone.conf ...

6. Best Practices for Easier Recovery in the Future

  • Keep snapshots — Avoid relying only on a single mirrored backup. Snapshots protect against accidental overwrites.
  • Separate configs for root and user — If backups are run with root, ensure the same config file is available when restoring.
  • Test recovery monthly — Randomly restore a few files to verify the process works.
  • Document your backup structure — Keep a map of where each directory is stored in the remote.

Final Thoughts

Using rclone crypt for encrypted backups gives you security, privacy, and flexibility — but recovery still requires you to know your backup layout and tools. By following a structured search → confirm → restore workflow, you can confidently recover lost files without exposing sensitive data or disrupting production services.

And remember: backups are only as good as your ability to restore them. Test them before you actually need them.

entry.title: Secure Your Backups with Rclone Crypt + S3
entry.summary: Overview Backing up critical data is essential, but encrypting that backup adds a much-needed layer of security. This guide will walk you through setting up automated, encrypted backups using rclone with the crypt backend and an S3-compatible storage like Tebi, Wasabi, or MinIO. Run: rclone…
entry.content:
Overview

Backing up critical data is essential, but encrypting that backup adds a much-needed layer of security. This guide will walk you through setting up automated, encrypted backups using rclone with the crypt backend and an S3-compatible storage like Tebi, Wasabi, or MinIO.

✅ Prerequisites

  • rclone installed (sudo apt install rclone)
  • Access to an S3-compatible storage service (e.g., Tebi)
  • Linux user with permission to run backups
  • A list of directories to back up (/etc, /home, /var/www, etc.)

🔧 Step 1: Configure the S3 Remote

  1. Run:

    rclone config

  2. Select n to create a new remote.

  3. Name: tebi-backup (or any name you like)

  4. Select storage type: s3

  5. Configure as follows:

    • Provider: Other
    • Access Key ID / Secret Access Key: As provided by your S3 host
    • Endpoint: https://s3.tebi.io
    • Region / Location constraint: Leave blank or default
    • ACL: private

🔐 Step 2: Create the Encrypted Remote (Crypt Layer)

  1. In the same rclone config, create a new remote (name it e.g., tebi-crypt)

  2. Storage type: crypt

  3. When prompted for the remote, enter:

    tebi-backup:crypted-storage-01

    Replace crypted-storage-01 with your encrypted bucket name.

  4. Choose encryption mode:

    • Filename encryption: standard
    • Directory name encryption: true
    • Set a strong password
    • Leave salt password blank or enter a second one for added security

📂 Step 3: Backup Script

Here’s an example bash script for encrypted backups:

#!/bin/bash

# Variables
REMOTE="tebi-crypt:backups"
LOG_FILE="/var/log/rclone-encrypted-backup.log"
TIMESTAMP=$(date "+%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M")

# Create log directory if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LOG_FILE")"

# Back up directories
rclone -P sync /home "$REMOTE/home-backup" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
rclone -P sync /etc "$REMOTE/etc-backup" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
rclone -P sync /var/www "$REMOTE/var-www-backup" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
rclone -P sync /DATA "$REMOTE/DATA-backup" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1

⏰ Step 4: Automate with Cron

Edit the crontab:

sudo crontab -e

Add:

30 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup-encrypted.sh

Ensure the script is executable:

chmod +x /usr/local/bin/backup-encrypted.sh

🔍 Step 5: Verifying Backups

To browse or retrieve files from the encrypted remote:

rclone ls tebi-crypt:backups/etc-backup
rclone copy tebi-crypt:backups/home-backup ~/restore/home --progress

📦 Optional: Mount the Encrypted Remote

To mount the encrypted bucket locally:

rclone mount tebi-crypt:backups /mnt/encrypted-backups --daemon

Install fuse3 if needed:

sudo apt install fuse3

To auto-mount at boot, add to rc.local or systemd.

🔐 Why Use Rclone Crypt?

  • Zero-knowledge: Your cloud provider never sees your plaintext
  • Encrypt filenames + contents
  • Works with any backend (S3, Google Drive, etc.)
  • Easy to integrate with automation

🧹 Tips

  • Test restore periodically
  • Rotate logs or archive monthly
  • Store rclone config securely (chmod 600 ~/.rclone.conf)
  • Backup your rclone.conf file!

entry.title: How to Set Up Automated Server Backups to Tebi.io with rclone
entry.summary: This guide explains how to configure a secure, automated backup system that uploads essential directories (like /etc, /home, /var/www, /DATA) to Tebi.io’s S3-compatible object storage, using rclone. curl https://rclone.org/install.sh | sudo bash 2. Configure rclone for Tebi.io Run: rclone config Then follow the prompts: Choose:…
entry.content:
This guide explains how to configure a secure, automated backup system that uploads essential directories (like /etc, /home, /var/www, /DATA) to Tebi.io’s S3-compatible object storage, using rclone.

🔧 Requirements

  • A Linux server (Ubuntu/Debian/CentOS tested)
  • rclone installed (v1.62+ recommended)
  • A Tebi.io bucket + S3 credentials (access key, secret key, and endpoint)
  • Root/sudo access

🛠️ Step-by-Step Setup

1. Install rclone

curl https://rclone.org/install.sh | sudo bash

2. Configure rclone for Tebi.io

Run:

rclone config

Then follow the prompts:

  1. Choose: n for new remote

  2. Name it: tebi-backup (or anything you like)

  3. Choose storage type: s3

  4. Provider: Other

  5. Enter your:

    • access_key_id
    • secret_access_key
    • endpoint: https://s3.tebi.io

  6. Region: Leave blank

  7. Location Constraint: Leave blank

  8. ACL: Choose private

When done, run rclone listremotes to verify:

tebi-backup:

3. Create the Backup Script

Create a new script:

sudo nano /usr/local/bin/tebi-backup.sh

Paste the following:

#!/bin/bash

REMOTE="tebi-backup:your-bucket-name/backups"
DATE=$(date +%F)
DAY=$(date +%u)
LOG_FILE="/var/log/tebi-backup.log"

echo "========== Backup started at $(date) ==========" >> "$LOG_FILE"

rclone -P sync /home "$REMOTE/home" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
rclone -P sync /var/www "$REMOTE/var-www" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
rclone -P sync /DATA "$REMOTE/DATA" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
rclone -P sync /etc "$REMOTE/etc" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1

if [ "$DAY" -eq 5 ]; then
  SNAPSHOT_DIR="$REMOTE/etc-snapshots/$DATE"
  echo "Weekly snapshot: /etc to $SNAPSHOT_DIR" >> "$LOG_FILE"
  rclone -P copy /etc "$SNAPSHOT_DIR" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1

  echo "Deleting old snapshots (>30d)..." >> "$LOG_FILE"
  rclone lsd "$REMOTE/etc-snapshots" --max-age 720h |
  awk '{print $NF}' |
  while read -r folder; do
    rclone purge "$REMOTE/etc-snapshots/$folder" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  done
fi

echo "========== Backup finished at $(date) ==========" >> "$LOG_FILE"

Replace your-bucket-name with your actual bucket.

Then make the script executable:

sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/tebi-backup.sh

4. Automate with Cron

Edit root’s crontab:

sudo crontab -e

Add this line to run backups daily at 2:30 AM:

30 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/tebi-backup.sh

📂 Folder Structure on Tebi

Your backups will be neatly organized like this:

backups/
├── home/
├── var-www/
├── DATA/
├── etc/
└── etc-snapshots/
    ├── 2025-07-05/
    ├── 2025-07-12/
    └── ...

🧪 Test the Backup

Run manually to test:

sudo /usr/local/bin/tebi-backup.sh

Then check:

rclone lsf tebi-backup:your-bucket-name/backups/

✅ Best Practices

  • Restrict Tebi.io S3 credentials to a backup-only IAM role.
  • Rotate your credentials every 90 days.
  • Encrypt backups at rest (Tebi supports server-side encryption).
  • Use rclone crypt if you want local encryption before upload.

entry.title: 🛠️ Migrating from Nginx Proxy Manager to Traefik – Part 2
entry.summary: 🌀 Traefik Comes Online Once Traefik was set up, I configured it with the following key features in the traefik.yml: entryPoints: web: address: ":80" websecure: address: ":443" providers: docker: exposedByDefault: false file: directory: /etc/traefik/dynamic watch: true certificatesResolvers: cloudflare: acme: dnsChallenge: provider: cloudflare email: example@example.com storage:…
entry.content:
🌀 Traefik Comes Online

Once Traefik was set up, I configured it with the following key features in the traefik.yml:

entryPoints:
  web:
    address: ":80"
  websecure:
    address: ":443"

providers:
  docker:
    exposedByDefault: false
  file:
    directory: /etc/traefik/dynamic
    watch: true

certificatesResolvers:
  cloudflare:
    acme:
      dnsChallenge:
        provider: cloudflare
        email: example@example.com
        storage: /letsencrypt/acme.json

This set the stage for dynamic config files and DNS-01 validation via Cloudflare.

🧱 Dynamic Configs for Each App

Instead of using Compose labels like Nginx Proxy Manager, I created .yml files in /etc/traefik/dynamic/ for each service. Here are some examples:

🔌 wol.yml

http:
  routers:
    wol:
      rule: "Host(`wol.example.site`)"
      service: wol-svc
      entryPoints:
        - websecure
      tls:
        certResolver: cloudflare

  services:
    wol-svc:
      loadBalancer:
        servers:
          - url: "http://host.docker.internal:9002"

📡 tenda-api.yml (No HTTPS)

http:
  routers:
    tenda:
      rule: "Host(`api.cloud.tenda.com.cn`)"
      service: tenda-svc
      entryPoints:
        - web

  services:
    tenda-svc:
      loadBalancer:
        servers:
          - url: "http://host.docker.internal:9001"

✅ Dynamic configs helped manage services independently and avoided bloating the Docker Compose.

🔐 Blocking External Access to Certain Ports

Instead of using a firewall to block apps like Pi-hole on ports like 53/82/85, I used binding tricks:

For Apache apps:

You can bind internal apps to localhost or internal IPs in Docker Compose or Apache:

Listen 127.0.0.1:82

Or Docker Compose:

ports:
  - "127.0.0.1:85:85"

That way, the service is inaccessible from outside but usable internally and by Traefik.

📦 Internal DNS Proxy (DoH)

I also had a dnsproxy DoH service that exposed port 5052. To hide it from public access, I updated the systemd unit:

ExecStart=/opt/dnsproxy/dnsproxy \
  -u https://cloudflare-gateway.com/dns-query \
  -b 1.1.1.1:53 -l 127.0.0.1 -p 5052

Binding to 127.0.0.1 ensures it can’t be reached externally, only locally.

📉 What Are EntryPoints like :8080?

By default, Traefik exposes a dashboard on port 8080. I didn’t want it public, so I either:

  • Disabled the dashboard completely.
  • Or protected it via IP whitelisting or basic auth using middleware.

📊 Metrics, Logs & Tracing

Traefik supports features like:

  • Access logs
  • Prometheus metrics
  • Jaeger tracing

To enable access logs in traefik.yml:

accessLog: {}

To enable Prometheus:

metrics:
  prometheus: {}

And for tracing:

tracing:
  jaeger:
    samplingServerURL: http://jaeger:5778/sampling

These helped monitor and debug routing and cert issues in real time.

🔍 Final Notes

Some lessons learned:

  • Don’t use 127.0.0.1 from inside containers to access host apps. Use host.docker.internal or a shared network.
  • ACME timeouts were mostly DNS issues or misconfigured firewalls.
  • Exposing internal-only services publicly is easily preventable with proper Docker port binding (127.0.0.1:port).

entry.title: Homelab Reverse Proxy Migration — Part 1
entry.summary: From Nginx Proxy Manager to Traefik: Hardening and Streamlining Services 📦 Introduction This guide documents the process of migrating from Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) to Traefik v2, while self-hosting several internal apps like: This migration is aimed at: Nginx Proxy Manager is a great GUI-based…
entry.content:
From Nginx Proxy Manager to Traefik: Hardening and Streamlining Services

📦 Introduction

This guide documents the process of migrating from Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) to Traefik v2, while self-hosting several internal apps like:

  • Pi-hole (network-level DNS filtering)
  • Vaultwarden (Bitwarden-compatible password manager)
  • Static sites served via Apache
  • Other services like WOL dashboards, API endpoints, and file managers

This migration is aimed at:

  • Improving TLS automation with Let’s Encrypt
  • Enabling fine-grained routing
  • Reducing open ports and tightening external access

🔁 Why Migrate from NPM to Traefik?

Nginx Proxy Manager is a great GUI-based solution but has limitations when:

  • Running multiple services on different ports
  • Needing automatic wildcard certificates
  • Enforcing advanced routing or middlewares
  • Wanting CLI/scriptable configuration

Traefik offers:

  • Native Docker integration
  • Automatic Let’s Encrypt TLS
  • Fine control over access and routing
  • Better performance and flexibility

🧱 Architecture Overview

Here’s the general layout of the stack:

Component Purpose Notes
Apache2 Hosts legacy apps on non-standard ports e.g., 9001, 9002, 85
Traefik v2 Reverse proxy and TLS termination Replaces Nginx Proxy Manager
Pi-hole Network-wide ad/DNS blocking Forwarded to port 53 internally
Vaultwarden Password manager Secured via HTTPS proxying
Docker Containerized services Shared network across services

🏗️ Apache Config (Non-Standard Ports)

You had several legacy apps hosted via Apache on specific ports like:

<VirtualHost *:9001>
  DocumentRoot /var/www/hear
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:9002>
  DocumentRoot /var/www/wol
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:85>
  ServerName file.domain.local
  DocumentRoot /var/www/html/tinyfilemanager
</VirtualHost>

❌ Problems with Exposed Ports

Some apps were exposed on ports like :85, :82, :9001, etc. which could be accessed externally unless firewalled.

To secure them without using iptables or UFW, we moved to this trick:

<VirtualHost 127.0.0.1:85>

Binding Apache to 127.0.0.1 ensures only localhost (and Traefik) can access those services. Docker containers can’t hit 127.0.0.1 of the host directly, so these are effectively isolated unless routed.

🔐 Traefik Now Handles All Public Access

Traefik is set up with:

entryPoints:
  web:
    address: ":80"
  websecure:
    address: ":443"
  traefik:
    address: ":8080"

Any apps exposed via Traefik now get:

  • Automatic TLS via Let’s Encrypt
  • Pretty subdomains (e.g., vault.domain.local)
  • Protected routing (optionally via middleware/auth)

You had to stop Apache from binding to :80/:443 to prevent port conflicts:

sudo systemctl stop apache2

Now Apache only handles internal routes; Traefik handles external.

📊 About Traefik’s Port 8080

Port :8080 is for the Traefik dashboard, useful for debugging during setup. You can restrict it later.

api:
  dashboard: true

entryPoints:
  traefik:
    address: ":8080"

To disable it in production, set api.dashboard: false and remove port 8080 from published ports in Docker.

🚧 Limitation: Docker Containers Can’t Access Host’s 127.0.0.1

You noticed this error inside a container:

wget http://127.0.0.1:85
# → connection refused

That’s expected — 127.0.0.1 inside Docker refers to the container itself, not the host.

To let Docker containers access the host:

  • Use the host’s internal bridge IP (e.g., 172.17.0.1)
  • Or on Linux, use extra_hosts in Docker Compose to map host.docker.internal
extra_hosts:
  - "host.docker.internal:172.17.0.1"

🌐 DNS & Pi-hole on Port 53

To make Pi-hole handle DNS for your network:

Option A: Use Docker’s published port

If Pi-hole is containerized:

ports:
  - "53:53/tcp"
  - "53:53/udp"

Option B: Forward using iptables (if DNS needs to stay centralized)

sudo iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p udp --dport 53 -j DNAT --to-destination <PIHOLE_IP>:53

🧪 Next Steps

You’re now at the halfway point of your migration. What’s working so far:

✅ Traefik is running and binds to ports 80/443 ✅ Apache is hidden from the outside ✅ TLS routing via Traefik is active ✅ Docker containers are network-isolated ✅ Pi-hole DNS is optionally routed

📝 Coming Up in Part 2

In the next section, we’ll cover:

  • 📂 Dynamic Traefik configuration (for Vaultwarden, Pi-hole, WOL, etc.)
  • 🔒 Basic auth / IP filtering middlewares
  • 🧼 Access logs, metrics, tracing
  • 🧭 Organizing the Traefik dashboard

Ready for Part 2?

entry.title: How to Use Vim: A Guide for Dummies
entry.summary: Hey there! If you’re new to Vim like me and feeling a bit lost, don’t worry i am too —this guide is written just for us :3. Vim is a super powerful text editor, but it’s not like the usual ones you might be used…
entry.content:
Hey there! If you’re new to Vim like me and feeling a bit lost, don’t worry i am too —this guide is written just for us :3. Vim is a super powerful text editor, but it’s not like the usual ones you might be used to (like Notepad or Word). It’s got a bit of a learning curve, but once you get the hang of it, you’ll feel like a text-editing wizard. Let’s break it down step by step, and I’ll keep it simple. Plus, there’s a handy cheat sheet at the end to keep you on track!

What is Vim?

Vim stands for “Vi Improved.” It’s a text editor that’s been around forever and is loved by people who code or work with text a lot. Why? Because it’s fast and you don’t need a mouse—everything’s done with the keyboard. That might sound weird at first, but stick with me—it’s worth it!

The Big Idea: Vim Modes

Here’s the trickiest part about Vim: it has different “modes.” Think of them like different hats Vim wears depending on what you want to do. You’ll switch between these modes all the time, so let’s meet them:

  • Normal Mode: This is where Vim starts. You use it to move around and give commands (like “delete this” or “copy that”).
  • Insert Mode: This is where you type stuff, like writing a sentence.
  • Visual Mode: This is for selecting chunks of text (like highlighting with a mouse, but cooler).
  • Command-Line Mode: This is for bigger commands, like saving your work or searching.

Don’t panic—we’ll learn how to switch between them next!

Step 1: Opening and Closing Vim

Let’s get started:

  • Open Vim: Open your terminal (that black box where you type commands). Type vim and hit Enter. Want to edit a file? Type vim myfile.txt.
  • Close Vim: This trips everyone up at first. Press Esc (to make sure you’re in Normal Mode), then type :q and hit Enter. If you’ve changed something and Vim won’t let you quit, type :q! to force it to close without saving.

Step 2: Switching Modes

Here’s how to move between those modes:

  • Normal to Insert: Press i. You’ll see “– INSERT –” at the bottom. Now you can type!
  • Insert to Normal: Press Esc. Back to command central.
  • Normal to Visual: Press v. Now you can select text with arrow keys or other movement keys.
  • Normal to Command-Line: Press :. You’ll see a colon at the bottom where you can type commands.

Step 3: Moving Around (Normal Mode)

In Normal Mode, forget your arrow keys for a sec—try these:

  • h: Move left
  • j: Move down
  • k: Move up
  • l: Move right

Want to zip around faster?

  • w: Jump to the next word
  • b: Jump back to the previous word
  • 0: Go to the start of the line
  • $: Go to the end of the line

Step 4: Typing Stuff

To write anything:

  1. Get into Normal Mode (press Esc if you’re not sure).
  2. Press i to enter Insert Mode.
  3. Type whatever you want.
  4. Press Esc to go back to Normal Mode.

Step 5: Editing Basics

  • Delete a letter: In Normal Mode, put your cursor on the letter and press x.
  • Delete a line: Press dd.
  • Delete a word: Put your cursor at the start of the word and press dw.

Step 6: Copy and Paste

  • Copy a line: In Normal Mode, press yy.
  • Copy a word: Cursor at the start of the word, press yw.
  • Paste: Press p. It’ll paste after your cursor.

Step 7: Oops! Undo and Redo

  • Undo: Press u in Normal Mode. Made a mistake? Fixed!
  • Redo: Press Ctrl + r to bring it back.

Step 8: Saving and Quitting

To save your masterpiece:

  1. Press : to enter Command-Line Mode.
  2. Type w and hit Enter (short for “write”).
  3. Want to save and quit? Type :wq and Enter.
  4. Changed your mind and want to ditch it? Type :q! and Enter.

Step 9: Finding Stuff

Need to find a word?

  1. In Normal Mode, press /.
  2. Type the word (like /hello) and hit Enter.
  3. Press n to jump to the next one, or N to go back.

Step 10: Selecting Text (Visual Mode)

  • Press v in Normal Mode to start selecting.
  • Move around with h, j, k, l to highlight text.
  • Then:
    • y to copy it.
    • d to delete (cut) it.
    • p to paste over it.

Tips to Survive Vim

  • Practice a little every day—it’s like learning to ride a bike.
  • Start small, like editing a grocery list.
  • Keep the cheat sheet below close by!

Vim Cheat Sheet

Here’s your quick guide to the basics:

What You Want How to Do It
Start typing i
Stop typing Esc
Save :w
Quit :q
Save and quit :wq
Quit without saving :q!
Undo u
Redo Ctrl + r
Delete a letter x
Delete a line dd
Delete a word dw
Copy a line yy
Copy a word yw
Paste p
Search for something /something
Next search result n
Previous search result N
Next word w
Previous word b
Start of line 0
End of line $

You’ve got this! Vim might feel strange at first, but soon you’ll be zooming around your files like a pro. Happy editing!

entry.title: GPG for Beginners: Sign, Encrypt, and Verify Like a Pro
entry.summary: You’ve probably seen this in hacker movies or privacy tools: -----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE----- That’s GPG (aka PGP). It’s real cryptography that you can use today — to sign, encrypt, and verify messages like a cybersecurity pro. Let’s jump in. Open your terminal and type:…
entry.content:
You’ve probably seen this in hacker movies or privacy tools:

-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----

That’s GPG (aka PGP). It’s real cryptography that you can use today — to sign, encrypt, and verify messages like a cybersecurity pro.

Let’s jump in.

🎯 Step 1: Generate Your GPG Key Pair

Open your terminal and type:

gpg --full-generate-key

When prompted:

  • Select RSA and RSA (default)
  • Choose 4096 bits
  • Set an expiration (or 0 for none)
  • Enter your name and email
  • Create a strong passphrase (you’ll need this to unlock your private key)

Done. You now have:

  • A private key (keep this safe!)
  • A public key (share it with the world)

🕵️‍♂️ Step 2: Sign a Message (Prove You Wrote It)

Create a simple file:

echo "This is a top-secret message" > message.txt

Now sign it:

gpg --clearsign message.txt

You’ll get message.txt.asc — a signed version readable by anyone.

🧪 Step 3: Verify a Signed Message

Let’s say someone sends you a .asc file. To verify it:

gpg --verify message.txt.asc

If you have their public key, GPG will tell you if the signature is valid.

🔐 Step 4: Encrypt a Message (Only Receiver Can Read It)

You want to send someone a private file.

First, import their public key:

gpg --import their-public-key.asc

Then encrypt:

gpg --encrypt --recipient their@email.com secret.txt

It outputs secret.txt.gpg, only readable by the recipient’s private key.

🔓 Step 5: Decrypt a Message (Sent to You)

If someone sent you an encrypted file:

gpg --decrypt secret.txt.gpg

You’ll be prompted for your passphrase. Then boom — message decrypted.

🌍 Step 6: Share Your Public Key

Want others to verify your signatures or send you encrypted messages?

Export your key:

gpg --armor --export your@email.com > mykey.asc

Now send that file, or upload it to a public keyserver:

gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --send-keys YOUR_KEY_ID

To get your key ID:

gpg --list-keys

🧠 Real-World Example: Signing a Statement

Let’s say you publish this:

I stand by this message 100%.

You sign it with GPG. Anyone can now verify that it really came from you and hasn’t been altered.

This is trust without needing a website or platform. Pure cryptography.

🧼 Clean Up: See and Manage Your Keys

List your keys:

gpg --list-keys

Delete a key (be careful!):

gpg --delete-secret-and-public-key your@email.com

💡 Final Thoughts

Using GPG isn’t about looking cool — it’s about owning your identity in a world of phishing and fake messages.

  • ✅ Signing proves “I wrote this.”
  • ✅ Encrypting ensures “Only you can read this.”
  • ✅ Verifying protects you from lies.

Get comfortable with these basics, and you’ll be ready for secure comms like a professional.
